utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, is it correct that at the beginning of that conflict in Mostar in September 1991 the JNA held the two predominant features, Velez and Hum, Velez is on the left bank of the Neretva and Hum on the right bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Croatian paramilitary forces took most of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's such a general question, I mean Mostar when? It is absolutely vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, could you ask the witness when the Croatian paramilitary forces took over Mostar. You say September 1991 and then we don't know, but it may be that the witness is not in a position to answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In September 1991 there was a conflict between the Croatian rebels and the JNA. Bosnia and Herzegovina was not at war yet at that time. The government of three national parties in coalition was functioning, the SDA, the Muslim party; the SDS, the Serbian; and the HDZ, the Croatian party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is not that now Mr. Seselj would testify himself as to the events that took place. He needs to seek information from the witness as to the date when the events. It was inadmissible because it was too vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Trial Chamber is already aware of what you say. You have to ask a question of the witness. Tell him: Witness, do you know that in September 1991 there was a conflict between the Croatian rebels and the JNA? And he anyway say yes, no, or I don't know, otherwise the Prosecutor will be on his feet saying you are testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be best for the Prosecutor to cross-examine instead of me. This is really pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I am not willing to let you manipulate the proceedings. There are rules. You are to conduct the cross-examination, and in this Tribunal cross-examination is governed by certain rules arising from Anglo-Saxon law. You are entitled to ask questions, but you're not allowed to testify through the questions you put. That is the difference, and if you are to testify systematically you're going to have objections from the Prosecutor and that will be a waste of time; you know that as well as I do. When the Prosecutor does not comply with Anglo-Saxon rules, you are the first one to object. Let us avoid this. Therefore, put your question in such a manner that even if you want to highlight an event you have to seek confirmation by the witness of the events through leading questions; that is authorised. That's it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now you've made me so frustrated with this initial noise that I don't even feel like putting questions, but I'll do my best. I didn't observe you yelling like that at representatives of the OTP, but that's up to you and your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are impolite, you are impolite, discourteous. You spent your time criticising everybody, including Judges; this is inadmissible. I reminded you what the rules were that prevail in this Tribunal. You may comply with them or turn them down. Everybody's got their own opinion, but that's the rules. Questions are put by the Prosecutor as part of the examination-in-chief and the Prosecutor is not entitled to testify, he is allowed to ask questions which he does in a non-leading way; and if he ever does, as you could see this morning, he is out of order by the Trial Chamber and you at times do the same. You criticise the Prosecutor for doing that. That's the Prosecution part of the examination. When cross-examination comes, you can ask any questions, but you're not entitled to testify. If you testify, the Prosecutor will be on his feet and will object. This is what I'm telling you now, and you do not want to admit it, but these are the rules.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue my cross-examination, I must first thank you for telling me that I'm impolite. I'm very grateful to you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, do you know what the JNA controlled on the west bank of the river Neretva apart from the hill of Hum before this conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podvelezje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we said that Podvelezje is on the west or east bank. The river Neretva divides Herzegovina into east and west Herzegovina and it's been like that for 500 years; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You controlled Siroki Brijeg up there, there were a lot of tanks up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, look, the army pulled out of that area. Siroki Brijeg is almost 100 per cent inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the army found it intolerable there because of the Croatian rebellion and the army pulled out of there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they may have been forced to leave because it was a large-scale uprising by Croats. So you are unable to say what else the JNA held on the west bank apart from the hill of Hum?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it correct that throughout September, October, November, December 1991 there was an exchange of fire between the JNA and Croatian paramilitary units across the river Neretva? The JNA was firing on one side and the Croatian paramilitary forces on the other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There were tanks underneath Podvelezje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, not just from Podvelezje. There was artillery firing from the west bank also. There was also sniper fire on both sides. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was artillery fire. Very well. And now, when Vance's plan was adopted it was towards the end of December 1991 there was a cease-fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a politician. I didn't concern myself with that truce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But for a while there was no shooting, there was a status quo, whoever was in control of certain area remained there. In 1992 was there fire in Mostar in January, February, March in 1992? Was there military activity?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean our side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there any shooting at all?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the army and the JNA collected the weapons from the civilian protection so that when they burst in no one had any weapons. The JNA collected all the weapons to prevent people from shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the civilian defence didn't have any weapons, it was the Territorial Defence that had weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In early 1991 the army took the weapons from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before the war in Croatia broke out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Slow down, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in January, February, and March 1992 in Mostar there was no fire on either side?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no fire until the tank truck exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear. Thank you very much. So it was the explosion of the tank truck in front of the wall of the JNA Barracks that was the signal for new armed hostilities?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the tank truck exploded --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- that's when the real war broke out?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's when I got back from the Gacko, from the field, it started from up there, from Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The explosion was so strong that it almost destroyed one of the barracks buildings and many surrounding civilian buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Many flats were damaged by the detonation and were unfit to live in; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When that happened you went to the atom bomb shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That atomic shelter was built for a real nuclear war?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it has an automatic door that would seal itself, it was a vast area where hundreds of people could take shelter and food could be kept there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were also devices to cleanse the air. So you were quite clear from nuclear, biological, or chemical weapons, even had they been used?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for nuclear and biological weapons and so on, not all the work had been finished, but there was enough air.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the artillery certainly couldn't harm you in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundreds of shells and tank shells and everything and mortar shells fell on the shelter, but they couldn't harm us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said thousands of shells fell?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there were two wars, one on each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I just said that those shells that fell on the shelter were fired from Podvelezje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, mostly from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did somebody target the shelter intentionally with artillery from Podvelezje?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs from up above, I don't know whether they saw what they were shooting at, but there were shells falling around about the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I assume the JNA from Podvelezje targeted Croatian positions and not their own forces and their own civilians?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both sides targeted this, in the Serb war and the Croatian war, they targeted the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just want to put right what you said in the examination-in-chief when you said that the shells were coming from Podvelezje and targeting your shelter, that's impossible, because the shells falling on your shelter were fired by the Croatian forces; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they began their war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But we said that the war began after the 3rd of April, the real war?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serb army hadn't withdrawn yet when the shells were still falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was still the JNA until the 19th of May, wasn't it, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The JNA targeted Croatian positions from the left bank and the Croatians from the right bank targeted the positions of the JNA and the inhabited settlements of civilians as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when you from Podvelezje targeted the Croatian side and some of our main buildings too were destroyed in town, Tito's Street, Razvitak and companies like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is Tito's Street on the west bank, the right bank?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our side under Podvelezje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Under Podvelezje, I see. Well then that was targeted by the Croats too, not the JNA. Why would the JNA target territory under its own control, there's no logic there, is there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was Croats and Serbs targeting, they both targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, both sides targeted but not themselves, they targeted the other side, the opposite side. Am I right? Why would you target yourself if you can target the enemy, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. I felt like asking the question Mr. Seselj just put whilst the Prosecution was questioning you, but I had some doubt as to who targeted the shelter. I even asked you this. I said were there Serbs in the shelter with you, and you said yes there was Serbs and Croats. So I wondered why Serbs would target their own Serbs. Now in his questions Seselj highlights the fact that it was the Croatian artillery that targeted the shelter. Do you agree with him on this point, on his idea, on his suggested explanation, namely, that when you were in the shelter the shells falling were fired by the Croats not by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I know is that the main road is above the shelter which leads to the sea, and on in fly-over on the main road there was a tank there all the time, the latest type of tank, the big type of tank, it was stationed there and didn't move until the Serbs withdrew. It was there all the time and did the shooting. Yes, it shot at the Croatian side and they had already united the Muslims and Croats to fight together; that's how it was. And then afterwards when they started shooting from up there, Podvelezje, that's when shells fell on the shelter, around the shelter. They would hit somebody's flat, kill a whole family, things like that, just any old which way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That shelter protected all of you, the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims, civilians from artillery and sniper fire, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the civilians were forbidden to move around except for the bare necessities, to go and fetch food or clothing or something like that, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you weren't allowed to move around because it was dangerous, a threat to your lives, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now we're progressing a little, we're making headway. Mr. Bilic, you were in that shelter from the 4th of April, which is the day after the explosion in front of the barracks, up until the 13th of June, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: April, May, June, that's almost two and a half months, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And your neighbours, the Serbs, how long were they in the shelter with you, the civilians?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there right up until we were taken away, until the bus came and took the Serbs away from the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was a little earlier, was it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The bus arrived much earlier than you were taken away to Sutina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were separated and sent to the bus and -- when I came back from Sutina to my flat, when I came back from Sutina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, it wasn't quite like that you said something different a moment ago. You said that the buses had arrived to take the Serbs away from the shelter and that they took the Serbs to Zijemlje which is an outskirt of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when I was saved, that day, that's when they were getting ready and preparing everybody --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Bilic, just a moment, let's take this step by step. This happened more than a month before the 13th of June, it happened sometime at the beginning of May, that's when that took place. And when the Serbs were taken away from the shelter the artillery fire stopped pounding the shelter. You told us that during the examination-in-chief, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So as soon as the Croats heard that the Serb civilians had left the shelter and that that remained were the Muslim and Croatian civilians, they stopped their artillery and sniper fire targeting civilian features, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you were able to leave the shelter and go about your work obligations, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well we worked, but there was still shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, you went to work where the sniper fire couldn't reach you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between the buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So your job was to clear up the rubble from the destroyed buildings, to deal with the rubble, the bricks and everything else --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I asked you to wait before you answer, and you're not doing so. Mr. Seselj is also firing questions at you even when you aren't finished answering, so because of this we have overlapping and we have a big problem with interpretation. So with this please try and wait before you answer, otherwise there's so much overlapping we cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just resolved the problem, Mr. President, that cropped up during the examination-in-chief, and you and the Prosecutor were unable to deal with it. When the Serbs left the shelter, the shelling stopped, and then it was possible for the work obligations to go ahead and for the people who were in the shelter and able-bodied men could be sent to do certain work and certain jobs, and that's the problem solved. That's that cleared up --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the witness said the opposite. He said that he started working when shelling was still going on, so Mr. Seselj is not using the witness's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you heard Mr. Seselj say that according to him when the shelling stopped you were able to go to work and people started to be able to move again. This is what Mr. Seselj is saying. The Prosecutor is saying that that is not the case. You're the only one to tell us what happened. Is Mr. Seselj right? Is he right? Is he wrong? If he's wrong, why is he wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he wasn't right. That's not when there was -- well, when the Serbs left. There was no work obligation then, after that. These were taken -- these people were taken to Sutina and that's when we worked, before we were taken to Sutina. And once they took us to Sutina there was nobody left to work, to do the work. All the people who could do some work had been killed. Only women and children and two or three elderly persons remained in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, given what the witness said, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In two places in Mostar you saw groups which you identified as being Seselj's men, Seseljevci, right? And that was in Luka or the port and the military institute, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You described them?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did you know that they were Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who led us, Savo, he said himself, These men are not from here, they're not ours, they're not our local people, they're people from up there, from Novi Sad, or rather, Serbia -- from far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The fact that they were from Serbia was sufficient for you to conclude that they were Seselj's men, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can tell by looking at them and, yes, they had big beards, they had insignia, markings, what else can I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they have a beard like me? What did you say, a beard like me?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't got a beard, just like me, I haven't got one either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how would they be Seselj's men by the fact that they wore a beard when I never wore a beard. Perhaps there was another way to identify them as being Seselj's men, not everybody wearing a beard can be identified as Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the others weren't capable or weren't responsible for what the others did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they were most capable for doing their job and that's why you thought they were Seselj's men, right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This answer is not satisfactory. Mr. Seselj is asking you whether just wearing a beard is sufficient to make you a Seselj's man. You're not answering that. Mr. Seselj adds that he himself is beardless, is clean-shaven. So through his question he's trying to highlight the fact that -- the connection, the possible connection between being -- having a beard and being a Seselj's man. You're not clear in your answer. When you say they were Seselj's men because those men had beards, does that mean that for you having a beard is sufficient to make anyone Seselj's man, but Mr. Seselj wears no beard? Do you understand my question or do you want me to reformulate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand it. Well, it -- they need -- it wasn't obligatory that they would have been Seselj's men, but I saw Seselj's men on television so that's why I thought it -- there were ten of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So we agree that you concluded that they were Seselj's men. Let's leave it at that, because they're similar to some people you saw on television. I'm satisfied with that answer. We don't have to dwell on that. But anyway, you had direct experience yourself with two men whom you also identified as being Seselj's men, right? And one of them was from Novi Sad together with you in the shelter, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he from the 4th of April right up to the 13th of June in the shelter with you, all that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came down from the Serbian church, when the soldiers surrounded us and he came and he was there from then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So from the 4th of April to the 13th of June he was there all the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He disappeared from Zalik, my wife told me, she was there, she was in the shelter. He left, they took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you knew that he was Seselj's man although he didn't have a beard?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he talked to us and he said he was from Novi Sad and was a Seselj's man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that; but he didn't have a beard, did he?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was in the shelter with you because he had a girlfriend, Vojo Pejanovic's daughter, and was she in the shelter with you too?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was but she was mostly in her flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But she was with him all the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were going out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this allegedly Seseljevci was in love and was with his girlfriend straight away and it didn't enter his head to go into battle?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was at the airport, he took her in an aeroplane or to aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that was his participation in the war, was it, going around with his girlfriend, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you said that when this man Seseljevci was in the shelter with you, that he sharpened his knife. Did he sharpen his knife every day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did nothing else but just kept quiet, was silent and sharpened his knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So for two and a half months he was sitting there sharpening his knife --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is impossible to translate at this speed. Thank you. Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj at line 18 the interpreters lost track of what you were saying so please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it a knife sharpener that you used or was it with -- was it an electrical appliance or what?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it was a grindstone, a wet stone, you did it by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was there sharpening his knife. All right. Now, if he sharpened his knife for two and a half months, that knife must have been as sharp as a needle, as thin as a needle?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't look at it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But you said these other Seselj men too whenever you would see them were sharpening their knives, the Seseljevci in the institute and in Luka?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whenever we passed by them, they would be sharpening their knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So whenever you came by they would take out their knives and start sharpening them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the answers of the witness because it's just too fast and overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You did your military service for a time, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you were issued a weapon, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have one then and I underwent training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't have undergone training without a rifle?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did it for the air force --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had to do infantry training, Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the aviation and technical service, so we didn't need a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But it was the M-48 rifles that were in use, the carbines, at that time, dating back to the 1950s and the 1960s that the army had?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they had rifles, but I really don't know what they had. I'm not well up on rifles, on weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, the people that you saw, what weapons did they have in their hands, the men you referred to as Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly those short automatics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or the AK-47, which was the JNA type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old type, you know, you would put the charge inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know the kind of bayonet that goes with a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about bayonets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you have a knife which is shorter than the classical type of bayonet but it's wider, precisely the type that you describe, the semicircle shaped knives that you mentioned, the Kama?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that's placed on a Kalashnikov for close-up fighting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have a long one on a rifle --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those are the old rifles with these long straight knives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, wait for the answer, please, and you're going much too fast and the interpreters are losing track.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've cleared that up as well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned another Seselj man who put a knife to your neck, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that was a dangerous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right, dangerous. And you said that you concluded that he was a Seseljevci because he was dangerous?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by his accent, he didn't speak like the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he speak like Serbs in Montenegro or like Serbs in Serbia, people in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't answer that, I don't know -- how should I know what part of Serbia he came from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I can understand that you're afraid and couldn't concentrate on that, but you should be aware that in Herzegovina itself people in certain areas speak with different accents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, for example, my mother and my father come from Trebinje municipality and they speak differently than people in Mostar do. People from Trebinje and people from Mostar don't speak the same way.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the differences aren't very great.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, but you can still tell where someone comes from by those differences?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I worked in Gacko I've worked in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So only by the fact that his accent was different did you conclude that this man who put a knife to your throat was a Seseljevci, you have no other reason for saying so?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Can we have on the ELMO the decision of the military court in Mostar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, I interrupted because the answer was not on the transcript, but now it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, I'll try to be finished with my cross-examination very quickly so that you are free to leave today. I see that you don't have a lot of patience for my questions and you don't really like answering them and I'll respect that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These comments are totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Bilic, that you are aware that the military prosecutor's office in Mostar in early 1993 submitted a criminal report against people who perpetrated the crime at Sutina; is that right, have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was an investigation into that crime?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said there was going to be an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Bodies were exhumed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And exhumation of bodies is always an investigative activity, right, so there was an investigation going on and in the course of the investigation the bodies were exhumed. At the motion of the district military prosecutor's office, the military district court in Mostar on the 2nd of March, 1993, issued an order on conducting an investigative procedure against 30 men. Is that on the screen? Yes. Now, please look at this list. You don't have to say any of the names out loud, just look through them and tell me whether there is a single man here who is not a local man from Mostar or the surrounding area. The first one is from Mostar, right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted), yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Don't say names because when you start mentioning names we'll have to move into closed session. So this second one is from Vrapcici, right, from Mostar, and the third one is from Mostar too. Please don't read the names out loud.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from Zalik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you can see the fourth one is from Mostar and so is the fifth one, the sixth one. Are you following?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The seventh one is from Mostar, right? What about the eighth one, is he from Mostar? It says Mostar --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they all lived in Mostar for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the next page, there are 30 in total. And they are suspected of having committed the crime in Sutina on the 13th of June, 1992. You see number 9, he's from Mostar as well, right, and then number 10, he's from Mostar, the 11th person is from Mostar, are you following me? Number 12 from Mostar. 13 is from Nevesinje. Have you come to number 13 yet?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nevesinje, very well. And then the 14th is from Mostar again, Vrapcici is in Mostar. The 15th also from Mostar, from Vrapcici, don't mention his name; you know him, but don't mention his name. The 16th is also from Mostar, is that right? And the 17th is from Mostar, you know him too don't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know almost all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Just don't mention their names.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know them from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, until there is a trial and until their innocence or guilt is proved, we won't mention their names. 18 and 19 are also from Mostar, number 20 is from Vrapcici, that's Mostar again, right. The 21st is from Mostar, the 22nd is from Mostar. Let's look at page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to page 3, please, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 23 is also from Mostar, right? 24 is from Mostar, 25 is from Mostar, 26 is from Mostar, 27 is from Mostar, Vrapcici; 28 is from Mostar, 29 is from Mostar, and 30 is from Mostar. They're all from Mostar except for one who comes from Nevesinje. Is that right? Can you see that, Mr. Bilic? Are you convinced?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about all of them, they're not all from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, all right, not all of them because one is from Nevesinje. Let me ask you this: The district military court in Mostar heard many people in connection with this crime. All the survivors and people who were able to know certain details in other ways, they also interviewed certain Serbs who lived in Mostar. They didn't call you, they didn't summon you, did they?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever summoned me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. They didn't summon you, but I will show you two statements by people who were interviewed in that investigation. One man is called Dervo Topalovic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bero, he was locked up in north camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he managed to survive by some miracle, so let's see his statement before the military court in Mostar, we're now dealing with the cantonal court in Mostar which took the proceedings over --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was trying to check, but I don't know whether these exhibits have been disclosed to the OTP. They might not have ever been disclosed to the OTP. I would like Mr. Seselj to let us know where these statements come from and whether these have been disclosed to the OTP, and if they have not been disclosed before the beginning of the hearing I object to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These statements I assume, Mr. Seselj, are statements given by people who are on the list that you must have had them because the Prosecutor disclosed these to you or the OTP did not disclose these to you and then you have got hold of them yourself. If you -- this did happen, did you disclose these to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor provided me with all of this but the problem is the OTP doesn't know what they gave me this is under Rule 65 ter 2569, page 4, it's the lady who acts in the registry has it. I think she can put it on the screen in English. The number is 2569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. Mr. Dutertre, Mr. Seselj has just told us that these documents come from the OTP. I had a question also on the topic. The Prosecutor from Mostar conducted an investigation and drew up an indictment which we have before us. What I would like to say is this: What happened to this case? Did the OTP look into the matter and see what has happened? When you look at the indictment like I do you can see that at the moment I wanted to read it out the indictment disappears from the screen. In this document it is mentioned that since April 1992 there are local Chetniks and there are members of the JNA who have committed whole series of offences which are listed here. Has the Prosecutor been made aware of this? Has he used this document? Has he checked what has happened to this or was there no follow-up to this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the document that Mr. Seselj would like to use, there are a great number of documents on its 65 ter list. We can't remember every single document that is in there. As far as the investigation conducted in Mostar is concerned, I will get back to you with accurate information as soon as I can because off the top of my head I would probably be wrong, and I had rather get back to you with the right information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, do you see that? Here at the top you see it's a statement made on the 29th of December, 2000, to the investigating judge of the cantonal court in Mostar, which means that the cantonal court took over this case from the military court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, now we have this statement before us. On the first page we have the basic data and then on page 2, Mr. Topalovic, turn to page 2, please, describes these events in similar way to the way you described them, of course two people can't describe an event in exactly the same way; but he gives his perception of this event and now on page 2 we can see that nowhere does he mention any Seselj's men. Dervo Topalovic whom I trust and whom I respect never mentions a single Seselj man. Can you see that not a single Seselj man is mentioned here? That's the only reason I'm showing this document, there's no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the exact question, Your Honour? I would like to know what the question is actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, on the basis of this document what is the question you are putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was very clear and concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Bilic, see anywhere in this statement made by Dervo Topalovic any mention of Seselj's men? Please go through the whole statement, it's a page and a half long, and confirm that nowhere does he mention Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his situation is one thing and mine is another. He didn't walk around, he didn't see things, he was constantly locked up in north camp until the Croats and Muslims came in and he was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. I have another statement here, it's a statement, it's page 6 of this same document; it's a statement by Admir Boloban also made on the 29th of December, 2000, to the investigating judge of the cantonal court in Mostar. Can we have that statement. Do you know Admir Boloban?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's go through his statement now. Please turn to the next page. His statement is somewhat longer, but on the next two pages, on the following two pages, we can see that he doesn't mention Seselj's men anywhere either. Can you see here that there's no mention of Seselj's men? Are you convinced?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness is asked to confirm something, please allow for enough time so that he can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this document is rather long. I have the English version and the B/C/S version. In a split second if Seselj's men are mentioned in the document this is something which you should be able to see, and seemingly this is not mentioned in the B/C/S text. Can you confirm this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm, but what I saw in Zalik and elsewhere, those insignia and all that, I can't say anything different from what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the difference between statements which are given to the investigators of this Tribunal or to any other entity for that matter, in this case there's an investigating judge -- in the year 2000, this statement was given in the year 2000, this was no war at that time and the investigating judge hears the witnesses. Any average investigating judge will try to find out who the perpetrators were, and the judge in question asks questions. And as you -- what you have before you is that the summary of the interview between you and your neighbour - and I'm sure that this judge who was a professional judge tried to understand what did what. Strangely enough in the document we have before us, Seselj's men aren't mentioned. Can you give us an explanation for this or not? Well, the witness answers those questions that have been put to him by an independent professional judge who wishes to get to the truth. So when this neighbour of yours sits in front of the judge, the judge wanted to find out who was there at the time. And the neighbour, your neighbour, doesn't mention anything about this. You were not confronted with this judge, but maybe you can provide an answer. Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admittedly, the indictment mentions the Croats solely. It was difficult perhaps to extradite people, but I wonder to what extent the witness can answer questions on statements which were made when he wasn't there and a situation with a judge which he knows nothing about, but I understand the purpose of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you answer this question, Witness? Why did your neighbour not mention Seselj's men when it could be very obvious? That could be the first thing he said to the investigating judge: Yes, these were Seselj's men, we were captured by Seselj's men. And this is not mentioned in the document, right? At the end I see that a soldier of the JNA in uniform, so he did give a number of details. Why doesn't he mention this? Perhaps you could say that you don't know if you don't know or maybe you have your reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. We won't dwell on this any longer, as we don't have a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, this statement that I received today from Belgrade, could you please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely the statement which I suggest should be shown at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj is trying to move on quickly so that the witness can go back home as quickly as possible. We shall do as best we can with the resources we have. Your associate speaks B/C/S; unfortunately, we have no such person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this will be interpreted by the interpreter, Mr. President, I hope that you too have concluded just as I have that this witness cannot hide his animosity towards me and that is why I want to cut short the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is totally inappropriate. I would like these comments to be put an end to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are not to make any conclusions. The Trial Chamber will draw its own conclusions when it has enough evidence before it. You have a Bench with professional Judges before you, so please trust them. So this is the text you would like to show. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, did you know Nedjeljko Bojanic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was born in Bogodol in the Mostar municipality, in 1956, and he lived in Zalik in the high-rise building from the beginning of 1991 up until June 1992 -- well, it's not really very clear here, you can't really read it. And he says, having provided some general information about Zalik, neighbourhood to the north of Mostar, along the -- between the main Sarajevo-Mostar road and the north camp barracks. He says that the population was mixed, just as you have told us, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and he says that the three peoples were there in about equal proportion. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A procedural issue. I have a four-page document, Your Honour. The fourth page which is a certified copy is illegible as it stands, so we cannot see and read whether there's a connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're not going to waste any time over this. You never can tell. It might prove useful. All we know is that in the local proceeding a statement is given and the statement is given by each individual. This is then certified. The Trial Chamber or the local court then certified it and it's signed and stamped. As my colleague as reminded us on several occasions, what is certified is only the signature. The stamp does not certify the content of the document in question. Everybody knows that. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, this gentleman here says that the north camp was publicly criticised by Muslims and Croats as a large stronghold of the JNA which advocated the survival of Yugoslavia and that's why protest marches were organized in front of the barracks with demands being made that the army move out. Do you remember those protest marches before the explosion took place?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago, I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. He says that there were regular soldiers and some reserves in the barracks, mostly Serbs and Herzegovina, which were in favour of keeping Yugoslavia together. And then he goes on to say about the tensions between the two polarised parties, Serbs were in the JNA and the Territorial Defence and Croats and Muslims were in their own Territorial Defence, the HOS, the Croatian armed forces, is that not right, and in their police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to really answer this question. It is a little bit complicated for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if it's complicated, then let us move on. He says that the armed conflict between the polarised parties occurred when the extremist from the Muslim-Croatian coalition attacked the barracks on the 4th of March, there may be a mistake made by either him or you, he says the 4th of March, you say the 3rd of March, but that happened around about that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then he says the attack was carried out at 1700 hours in such a way that a tank truck was brought in from Bijelo Polje, it was full of explosives and various pieces of iron, it was parked next to the largest building in the north camp barracks where the soldiers' quarters were located. Since at that time the troops were resting in the dormitory, it was obvious what the objective was. The explosion was so destructive that it fully destroyed the military dormitory and caused substantial damage to the other buildings close by in the barracks, and civilian facilities that were across the road from the barracks. At the time of the explosion I was outside of my building and my sister was in the apartment with small children. They survived by mere miracle. My building, 12 storeys, 64 apartments, was fully demolished and most of the surrounding buildings were damaged. When this explosion took place over 70 civilians were wounded and two Croats who were passing by in a vehicle were blown to pieces. Fortunately only one soldier was severely injured in the dormitory, but he soon died. Is this an accurate description, Mr. Bilic? You don't want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. So that's how it was. And then he goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is kindly asked to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand that he wants to go fast and release the witness, but he reads a long bit and then he makes 10 or 15 proposals and asks the witness whether that's right. So when the witness says yes we don't know what he says yes to. It might be better to break it down. I know we are under time constraints. We also need to have re-direct. So let's have some sense in this. Because the answer yes, we don't know what it is yes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, please could you ask for some explanation. What does he say yes to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The description of the situation, the consequences of the explosion. One building was fully demolished and the others were damaged, the barracks building almost completely destroyed. That's what the witness provided his answer to, and he says well more or less that was it. He didn't give us a very decisive answer, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. So when the troops started clearing up the rubble looking for the victims, not knowing who was in the dorm at the time, gun-fire was opened on them, first from the Orlac neighbourhood across the Neretva river and then from the residential buildings in Zalik. It was quite clear to us that this was a coordinated attack carried out in order to destroy the army. After this day mortar and artillery attacks from the other bank of the Neretva River controlled by armed Croatian Muslim units owned the troops in the barracks were a daily occurrence so that several soldiers were injured and there were even people who were killed including a neighbour of mine Milenko Ivanisevic. Do you know about this fire being opened from the Croatian Muslim side and the killing of Ivanisevic, this soldier by the name of Ivanisevic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. He goes on to say: "In the evening fire was opened from rifles in the residential buildings in Zalik, that was a JNA-controlled area, on the soldiers on the barracks resulting in injuries to three soldiers. For this reason we, the loyal civilians, were asked by the army command in the barracks to assist them to identify the assailants, but this did not help. I know that after two soldiers were injured or wounded the reservist soldiers from the barracks organized a search of the houses and apartments and there was a pair of brothers, I think their last name was Kuko, who had a house above the main road. They found some rifles and the barrels were still hot. They were as far as I could hear from the others arrested and taken away to the military prison in Bileca. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the suspicion that they attacked the army with snipers?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes we, that's quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After this comprehensive search of the apartments in Zalik that was -- that were close to the barracks, the shooting incidents involving the army became less frequent but there were such instances. Soon after that, there was a complete blockage of the bridges on the Neretva River, the Muslim and Croatian population in the part of Mostar south of the railway station mostly crossed to the right bank of the Neretva which was controlled by the Muslim-Croatian units, and -- but in Zalik most of the population remained on the right bank. Since there were daily -- there was daily shelling on the barracks and the Zalik neighbourhood which was close to the barracks, the population for the most part moved to two atomic shelters. They were together there, Serbs and the others. As for the food supplies it was difficult and there was only one shop that was next to the Matkovici -- or rather, it was owned by Matkovici, but at any rate they were selling food to most people.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you buy stuff from them?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. And then he goes on to say: "For those reasons the barracks command ordered that everybody should be in the barracks and that a list of all people in Zalik should be made and to control whether they were present in the shelters in the evenings. Some civilians were in charge of making those checks. I personally did not know them because I had spent a short time in Zalik. I know that everybody moved around freely during the day, went to their apartments, and in the evening there was a curfew in place. And movement through the neighbourhood was prohibited for all those who were not members of the military or the TO. At the Matkovic place there was a group of people, mostly his neighbours, from the village and from Zalik who in collaboration with the military maintained law and order in this neighbourhood. This situation lasted until the JNA withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since Croats and Muslims who were in Zalik were not in the army, a request was made to put them in work units, to clear up the main road Marsala Tita's Street which was impassable because of the rubble caused by the fighting." And he goes on to say that: "The local police was also involved," to cut a long story short and he doesn't know if there were any other jobs to be done apart from this one. And that this street was deep behind the confrontation lines and that people working there were not exposed to direct sniper fire from the other side. And then this is important: "In the Zalik area there were no volunteer units from outside, not even Seselj's men. The only armed units were those that belonged to the JNA, to the TO, and several police officers" --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we know what the question is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will learn that in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but upon reading all this the witness is bound to get confused and so are the Judges. I mean, they've lost it already some of them. So please break it down in various questions, otherwise we get lost, because now you're moving on to another topic which is the issue of Seselj's men, whilst before we had a description. You should have finished by saying: So this is the description given by that man, do you agree or not, and he would have given you an answer, yes, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I simply skimmed this over, rephrasing it, to come here to the point where this eye-witness says there were no volunteer units from the outside and there were no Seselj's men in Zalik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this true, Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I can tell you is that there in the Matkovic shop there was the staff and there was a machine-gun on the top of that house. That's all I know, all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. He says the only armed units were those belonging to the JNA, TO, and several police officers. It was hard to get to Zalik from the south zone where the Mostar Municipal Assembly was because a part of the road from the Orthodox church by the Sarica cemetery and the mosque was daily -- was almost impassable during the day because it was exposed to the sniper fire from the other bank of the Neretva river, is that correct, that it was impossible to get to the municipality by the day because of the sniper fire from the other bank of the Neretva river. You don't know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, well there was fire coming from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. As far as I know four civilians were killed by this fire who moved to the southern part on their own risk and -- well, this might be of importance to you. The Serbian Territorial Defence for all intents and purposes did not have any military uniforms. They often wore combined civilian and military clothes, there were no -- there was no strict command or any orders to cut their hair or beards so that there were people with long beards and long hair. Everybody did whatever they pleased. Some of them obtained military uniforms through different channels, some wore American boiler suits, camouflage, or single-colour, it was complete -- a complete mess in this respect. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were many people fleeing from the army ranks and throwing down -- throwing away their uniforms. So you could find those parts of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. So now he talks about the withdrawal of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as this began people started deserting, some of them, they went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he says after the JNA withdrew, the all-out attack from the Croatian-Muslim side started on the 13th and the 14th of June. Do you know about this attack and the breakthrough from Capljina to Stolac and Mostar from the south?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that there were people talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says that the left bank of Mostar was defended by Serbs, territorials, who were not used to fighting and there was -- there were a lot of casualties, some people were wounded, some were killed, and there was chaos?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well the fighting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he's talking about the withdrawal towards Vrapcici and Bijelo Polje and he says at that time the Muslims attacked the command of the Serbian army in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please read slowly. It is impossible to interpret at this rate of speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stopped you because the interpreter was lagging behind. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's hard to follow. I will have some very few brief questions in re-direct, so if we want to release the witness, we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj keeps that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will complete my examination right now so that the Prosecution will have a chance to do the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please turn the next page and here Mr. Nedjeljko describes the chaotic situation. Could you please move it a little bit. And then he says about the mass withdrawal from the whole Neretva valley, he says that for the most part all the houses in the Neretva valley were burned, that Serbs there were killed. Have you heard about that, that all Serbs in the Neretva valley, all the Serbs that were found by the Croatian-Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't heard about that. I didn't go there, I couldn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he says: "Later on I learned that Muslims were killed in this withdrawal, those who found themselves in the shelter in Zalik, and for me and my colleagues this -- we took it as a great shame for us because this had not been the practice of the Serb army that far. He says he doesn't know how many people were killed and we know why, but he says that as far as he knew this was a reprisal for those who were killed in Vrapcici by their fellow fighters and this was the consequence of the chaotic situation and the absence of chain of command and the resignation after the loss of positions." So this is his explanation why this crime against Muslim civilians occurred. Do you think this lie as a basis, a motive, I'm not trying to a justify a crime, a crime is a crime; but were those the motives of the people who perpetrated the crimes? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that. I would be more in favour of saying it was genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bilic, if you say genocide, you have to know what this implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That you would observe all over Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this completes my examination. I wanted to go into some other things, but in order to give some time to the Prosecution for the re-direct, I will complete my examination now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Your re-direct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to refer to transcript pages. You heard the cross-examination. You said that Serbs, Mr. Bilic, were evacuated from the basement prior to the 13th of June, that's what was said in cross-examination. Could you tell us why -- why the Serbs did not evacuate you as well, you and the Croats who were in the basements, was it out of humanity? Did --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Why the Serbs did not evacuate you, as they did evacuate their Serb fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had already been taken to Sutina and there were just the women and children who remained there. When I got back from Sutina I saw buses picking up Serbs and only women and children remained. I saw the bus in front of the shelter, it was white, a large white bus and they headed up there towards Zijemlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand. So the Serbs being evacuated from the basement where you were, that happened on the day when you went to Sutina, is that how I should understand?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when I got back from Sutina, that was one day and one night. Just before dawn I saw the bus taking away the Serbs, I saw them board the bus to be taken away, and I saw them from my apartment because I had already taken shelter in my apartment just around the corner. That's where I spent four days and four nights without anything to drink or anything to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And up until that day, had the shelter been shelled, had there been artillery fire up until that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, after I got there, there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay, but had there been shelling until the day when you were taken out of the basement to be taken to Sutina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, shells were falling up until that time. We couldn't go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Regarding this person who is -- who says he's a Seselj's man in the basement. When he said so, that he was a Seselj's man, how far were you from him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we sat right next to it. There was a group of us. We were sitting next to him. There were about ten of us there. I wasn't alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you returned around the 14th, returned to your apartment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous question was tendentious. Perhaps this soldier was Seselj's man in order to have success with women, not to fight a war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know that. You should ask him, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you returned to your home after having spent the night of the 13th to the 14th in Sutina, you stayed there some time. But tell us, were the Serbs still there in Zalik, at around Zalik, or was the attack of the Croatians already started?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a flat around the corner and they were still guarding the north camp, and four or five days later, after they took away the Serbs, after some four or five days, they came -- our people came from the other side and came to the north camp and then the Serbs withdrew with their vehicles and everything in the direction of Zijemlje and they all withdrew, the civilians, the Serb civilians, and the soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: My last question. When you were forced to do labour outside, was there artillery shooting, was there shooting from the artillery or shooting from snipers, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN BILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A shell would fall close to us, but nobody was actually targeting us. We were doing our job cleaning up, loading up on to a truck. Sometimes our men would climb up on to the truck to make the garbage more compact and they would fall from it and break their arm. Things like that happened. These were Vranica trucks belonging to the Vranica Construction Company from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, thanks to the Prosecution and to the Defence's help, we were able to finish today, you don't have to stay over the weekend. I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague to testify, and I wish you a safe return home. And now talking to Mr. Seselj and to the Prosecution we have the witness scheduled for three days, and we will be sitting in the afternoon. Therefore, we meet again on Tuesday at 2.15 p.m. I wish Mr. Seselj's associates a safe return home also. They came here to attend this hearing today. Thank you all, and we'll meet again on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of July, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
